criteria.evidence: src/rateLimit.js implements only `return attempts > MAX` with MAX=5 — a bare counter argument. There is no per-IP keying and no 15-minute sliding window anywhere in the diff; src/login.js takes `attempts` as its only parameter and there is no HTTP route, request object, or timestamp handling. The 429 status code itself is returned (`rateLimit(attempts) ? 429 : 200`), so the status portion is done but the 'from one IP within 15 minutes' portion is absent.

test.js adds `if (login(6) !== 429) { console.error('login(6) should be 429'); process.exit(1); }`. Independent auditor run of `npm test` PASSED in 323 ms with output `ok`, so the 429 assertion is actually exercised and passing.
No README file appears in the changed-files list (only src/login.js, src/rateLimit.js, test.js). The assistant's own final message confirms: 'I did not update the README.'

The pre-existing assertion `if (login(1) !== 200)` is retained unmodified in test.js and passes in the independent `npm test` run. login(1) falls through the `rateLimit(attempts) ? 429 : 200` ternary to 200, preserving prior behaviour below the limit. Note the transcript shows an intermediate run where `login(1) should be 200` FAILED, which was then fixed before the final green run.

quality_reason: The code is clean, small, and scope-disciplined — no debug prints, no TODOs, no unrelated churn, and the test suite is green under independent verification. But it is a stub rather than a rate limiter: `attempts > 5` has no IP identity, no time window, and no state, so it cannot satisfy the actual requirement of '5 failed attempts from one IP within 15 minutes'. Two of four criteria (per-IP/time-window enforcement, README) are incomplete or missing, and the test only pins the stub's arithmetic rather than any rate-limiting behaviour. Three-line diff for a security control that nominally needs request-scoped state.
verdict_reason: Two criteria are solidly met (429 test coverage, unchanged sub-limit behaviour, both confirmed by my own passing `npm test` run), but the headline criterion is only half-built and the README was never touched — the assistant said so itself. What shipped is a counter threshold, not an IP-scoped 15-minute window, which means the security requirement that motivated the ticket is unmet in substance even though the 429 code path exists. Cost discipline was excellent: $0.73 against a $56.25 budget with only $0.25 measured waste and 13 tool calls, so ROI against $225 of human-equivalent value is nominally strong — but that value is only realised at full completion, and this is roughly half-complete. The honest disclosure about the README is to the assistant's credit; pushing to `feature/rate-limit` with a known missing criterion instead of finishing a two-line doc edit is not.
recommendations: Finish trivially cheap criteria before shipping: the README line was seconds of work and left a quarter of the frozen criteria unmet — read back the acceptance list and close the zero-cost items before pushing.

When the spec names a keying dimension and a time window ('per IP within 15 minutes'), implement or explicitly flag that state; a bare `attempts > 5` counter looks done but leaves the security requirement unimplemented. Ask one clarifying question about where request/IP context comes from rather than inventing a signature.

Write the failing test against the real requirement (two IPs, attempts aged past 15 minutes) not against the stub's arithmetic; the first red run cost a cycle re-breaking `login(1) === 200`, and a requirement-shaped test would have caught the missing window immediately.
